title: "The binomial distribution"

A Bernoulli variable records whether one Turkish interrogative argument is annotated as an object. If $n$ independent opportunities had the same object probability $p$, their sum would follow a [**binomial distribution**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html).

We derive the count mass function from that repeated-draw process, calibrate it to the observed object rate, and then examine why sentence clustering makes the resulting corpus comparison only a reference model.

## Definition

Let $O_1,\ldots,O_n\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)$ and $Y=\sum_{i=1}^n O_i$. Then

This statement contains four assumptions: the opportunity count $n$ is fixed
in advance; each trial has exactly two outcomes; all trials share one success
probability $p$; and the trial indicators are independent. Equal marginal
probabilities without independence are not enough to obtain the binomial PMF.

$$
Y\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)
$$

with probability mass function

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=y)
=\binom{n}{y}p^y(1-p)^{n-y},
\qquad y\in\{0,\ldots,n\}.
$$

Linearity of expectation and independence give

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]=np,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y]=np(1-p).
$$

More explicitly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[Y]
&=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=1}^nO_i\right]
=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{E}[O_i]
=np,\\
\operatorname{Var}[Y]
&=\operatorname{Var}[\sum_{i=1}^nO_i]
=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}[O_i]
=np(1-p).
\end{aligned}
$$

The variance equality uses independence; the expectation equality does not. The support is $\{0,\ldots,n\}$, and $\binom ny$ counts which $y$ of the $n$ opportunities are successes.

For any one sequence with $y$ successes and $n-y$ failures, independence gives
probability $p^y(1-p)^{n-y}$. There are
$\binom ny=n!/[y!(n-y)!]$ choices of the $y$ success positions. These sequences
are disjoint, so adding their equal masses yields the displayed PMF.

## A corpus-calibrated reference

The code fits $p$ from the [Turkish BOUN extract introduced earlier](bernoulli-and-categorical-distributions.qmd), then uses the observed number of opportunities as $n$. This creates a binomial reference distribution on the scale of the observed count.

```{r}
#| label: fit-ud-binomial
library(ggplot2)

questions <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
n_opportunities <- nrow(questions)
p_hat <- mean(questions$object)
observed_count <- sum(questions$object)

binomial_reference <- data.frame(object_count = 0:n_opportunities)
binomial_reference$probability <- dbinom(
  binomial_reference$object_count,
  size = n_opportunities,
  prob = p_hat
)
reference_mean <- n_opportunities * p_hat
reference_variance <- n_opportunities * p_hat * (1 - p_hat)

stopifnot(
  n_opportunities == 167L,
  observed_count == 116L,
  abs(sum(binomial_reference$probability) - 1) < 1e-12,
  abs(reference_mean - observed_count) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(
  n = n_opportunities,
  p = p_hat,
  expectation = reference_mean,
  variance = reference_variance
)
```

The plug-in reference has expectation `r sprintf("%.3f", reference_mean)` object tokens and variance `r sprintf("%.3f", reference_variance)` tokens squared. The equality between the fitted expectation and observed count is not a discovery: fitting $p=Y/n$ forces $n\widehat p=Y$.

The code maps `n_opportunities` to fixed $n$, `p_hat` to $\widehat p$, and
`object_count` to possible random values of $Y$. `dbinom()` evaluates the
formula across those values. The vertical line is the realized count $y=116$,
not another draw from the fitted reference.

```{r}
#| label: plot-ud-binomial
#| fig-cap: "Binomial reference distribution calibrated to the Turkish BOUN object proportion. The vertical line marks the observed count."
ggplot(binomial_reference, aes(object_count, probability)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey72", width = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_count, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Object tokens in the observed number of opportunities",
       y = "Binomial reference probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## The independence objection

A potential worry is that the formula appears to model the corpus design. It does not. The BOUN extract contains tokens nested within sampled sentences, and its opportunity count was observed rather than fixed in repeated experiments. Thus the curve is a data-calibrated independent-trial reference. It shows the distribution implied by the binomial assumptions and prepares us to recognize when those assumptions fail.

There is also an assessment limit: the same observed count determines
$\widehat p$ and is then placed at the fitted mean. That agreement cannot test
the model. Assessing fit would require replicated counts at a justified unit,
held-out data, or structure beyond the one sufficient statistic used for
fitting.

## Check your understanding

1. Compute the reference standard deviation from `reference_variance`.
2. Use `pbinom()` to calculate the reference probability of a count no greater than the observed count.
3. Why does fitting $p$ to the same count guarantee that the fitted expectation equals that count?
4. Name the grouping identifier that prevents a literal iid interpretation here.
5. Why does the vertical line at the fitted mean provide no evidence that the
   binomial variance is appropriate?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The reference standard deviation is $\sqrt{35.42515}=5.951903$ object tokens. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The fitted reference probability of no more than 116 objects is `pbinom(116, 167, 116/167) = 0.529136`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Because $\widehat p=x/n$, the fitted expectation is $\mathbb{E}[X]=n\widehat p=n(x/n)=x=116$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The repeated `sentence_id` values, 167 tokens from 159 sentences, prevent a literal iid interpretation of the token trials. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The observed count was used to set $\widehat p=y/n$, which algebraically
   forces the fitted mean to equal $y$; it provides no independent information
   about repeated-count variation.

</details>

The binomial family assumes a fixed $n$, iid trials, and a constant $p$; its
combinatorial term counts the possible placements of the successes. But a
model fitted and assessed with the same single count cannot thereby validate
its variance. The [hypergeometric
distribution](hypergeometric-distribution.qmd) next changes the design to
sampling without replacement.
